title: Depression years, copying Ellington records and Mercer's explanation of Duke's triads
summary: Copying Blue Ramble off the record, miswriting chords, and years later learning from Mercer Ellington that Duke scored in stacked triads.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: It was difficult, living in the San Joaquin Valley. The other kids in town were interested in music but not to the extent I was. And not having any money, this is the Depression

years, my father was out of work for several of those years. There wasn't that much jazz coming out to California anyhow. As Wingy Manone once said, it never got over the Rocky Mountains. But about once a month one Armstrong record would come out and one Duke Ellington record would come out. And some way I would beg, borrow or even steal, truthfully, for one of these records. And I started copying off -- also tried to copy off the Duke Ellington records.

I didn't know anything about harmony or anything but I knew the names of triads. So if I had what I guess you would call a C ninth, that -- a C 13th. I remember "Blue Ramble" is the first tune I copied and the chord -- and I had a C, A, E, G, D, B flat, see, in the bass. So I called that a G minor chord and A minor chord with C in the bass.

Now, years later I was copying off some of those records for Mercer Ellington because they had lost the arrangements in the band. And I was telling him when I was young how I'd written chord symbols, I didn't know how to write them. I said, I'd write A minor, G minor with C in the bass. And he kind of laughed and I said, what's funny. He said, that's what Poppa did.
And he explained that Duke wrote everything in triads, which was interesting. Because when I copied the records, I could follow each part. And I would hear the three trumpets

going C, A, E down. But above the third trumpet would be the trombone playing in G. And I couldn't figure out why he was doing that. And after Mercer explained to me that he wanted a perfect triad of an A-minor in the trumpets and a G-minor in the trombones, that's how the G got over the third trumpet. And that clarified a lot of copying arrangements later, when I couldn't be sure what I was hearing. If I followed that principle, it would come out right. Because Duke had told -- he said that he wanted every section to sound good by itself so that he had no rubs, you know, people playing half-steps apart or full steps apart.

So the first record I copied was "Blue Ramble." And it must have taken me six months to copy that thing and I couldn't get anybody to play it anyhow. You know, the kids in high school sort of -- they weren't that interested in playing.
